title: Eliphaz Names Job's Crimes
sum: Eliphaz opens the third round with his harshest speech. God gains nothing from human goodness, he says, so Job's suffering cannot be for his piety; it must be for great sin (22:2–5). Then he invents the sins: Job took pledges for no reason, stripped the poor, refused water to the weary and sent widows away empty (22:6–9). He accuses Job of thinking God cannot see through the clouds (22:12–14) and warns him of the ancient path of the wicked whom a river swept away (22:15–20).

The speech ends with a warm call to come back to the Almighty. If Job puts away wrong and treats gold as dust, God will be his treasure, will hear his prayers, and will even rescue the guilty through Job's clean hands (22:21–30). The last line comes true in a way Eliphaz never imagined: at the end, God tells Eliphaz that Job will pray for him (42:7–9).
readings: Read as the friends' theology at its limit

Eliphaz's logic is airtight if its premise is true: God is just, so suffering is deserved. Since Job suffers greatly, he must have sinned greatly. With no evidence, Eliphaz supplies the sins. The speech shows where a theology of strict reward and punishment leads when it meets an innocent sufferer: it must slander him to stay intact.
Read as pastoral advice

Taken apart from its charges, 22:21–30 is a fine call to repentance, close to what Israel's prophets and psalms say (Isaiah 55:6–7; Hosea 14:1–2). Many readers have used it that way. The book's frame warns against applying it to Job, whose suffering has a cause no one on earth knows (1:6–12).

views.H: Eliphaz the Temanite comes from Teman in Edom, a region famous for wise men (Jeremiah 49:7; Obadiah 8). Traditional readers take this as a real debate among real sages, recorded in poetic form.
views.C: Most critics see the speeches as the work of one poet who gives each friend a voice. Eliphaz's speech is the clearest and most complete in the third round, which is one reason scholars think the rest of the round has been damaged (see the deep dive below).
views.W: The Babylonian Theodicy, a dialogue between a sufferer and his friend (about 1000 BC), has the same structure: the friend insists that the one who serves the god prospers and accuses the sufferer of blasphemy, while the sufferer points to wicked men who thrive. Like Eliphaz, the friend ends by urging him to seek the god's favor.
views.J: The Talmud reports a view that Job's suffering came from his own fault: Rava said Job "sought to turn the dish upside down," to declare the whole world free from judgment (Bava Batra 16a). Rashi takes the river of 22:16 as the Flood, or the fire of Sodom. Maimonides sees Eliphaz as the voice of the view that all suffering is punishment for sin, the view of the Torah as commonly taught, which he thinks incomplete (Guide 3.23).
views.X: Gregory the Great read Eliphaz as the type of those who teach true things wrongly applied. Calvin, in his Sermons on Job, says much of what the friends say is true doctrine, but they used it to crush a man God had not condemned. The charge list (22:6–9) is close to the works Jesus names in Matthew 25:35–45.

deep.b:
The first two rounds of speeches are complete: each friend speaks, and Job answers each one (chapters 4–14 and 15–21). The third round begins the same way, with Eliphaz (22) and Job (23–24). Then things go wrong. Bildad speaks only five verses (25:2–6). Job answers him (26:1–4), but goes on with a hymn that sounds like a friend's (26:5–14). Job then begins again with a new formula (27:1) and in 27:13–23 describes the doom of the wicked in Zophar's own words (20:29). Zophar never speaks. Earlier, in 24:18–24, Job also seems to say what his friends say. Readers have explained this in three main ways.

1. The text was damaged and put back together in the wrong order. This is the most common view among critical scholars. Pages or columns of an early scroll were lost or shuffled, and a later scribe gave all the remaining speeches to Job. Scholars rebuild the third round in various ways. A typical reconstruction: Bildad speaks 25:1–6 and 26:5–14; Job answers in 26:1–4 and 27:1–12; Zophar speaks 27:13–23, often with 24:18–24 (Dhorme, Pope, and with variations Clines and many others). Some also give 27:7–12 to Zophar. The New American Bible (1970) printed a rearranged order. Supporters point to the broken pattern, the new heading at 27:1, and Job's sudden agreement with the friends. Against it: no manuscript has any other order. The Old Greek follows the Hebrew sequence, though it is much shorter in exactly these chapters: it lacked 24:14b–18a, 26:5–11, 26:14a, 27:19b and 27:21–23, which Origen filled in from Theodotion, and its 24:18b–24 is a curse on the wicked rather than a description (checked in the NETS translation). The Aramaic Targum from Qumran (11QtgJob) has columns covering parts of 24:12–17, 24:24–26:2, 26:10–27:4 and 27:11–20, in the Hebrew order (as reconstructed by Zuckerman and Reed; the official edition, DJD 23, was not consulted). That shows only that the order was in place when the Targum was translated, which is usually dated to the second or first century BC. It cannot show whether the order is original.

2. Job is quoting his friends, or speaking with irony. Robert Gordis argued that biblical poets often quote another person's view without saying "you say." Read this way, 24:18–24 and 27:13–23 are Job holding up the friends' doctrine to show its emptiness, or turning it against them: if the wicked really suffer like this, you who accuse me falsely should be afraid (27:7). Some translations (RSV, ESV) insert "You say" at 24:18. Supporters note that speakers in Job do quote each other (Eliphaz quotes Job in 22:17–18). Against it: nothing in the Hebrew marks the quotation, and the passages are long.

3. The breakdown is deliberate. Literary readers such as Francis Andersen, J. Gerald Janzen and Edwin Good keep the text as it stands and read its shape as meaning. The friends have run out of arguments: Bildad can only repeat a line Eliphaz has already used (25:4; 4:17; 15:14), and Job interrupts him. Zophar's silence speaks. Job's words in 27:13–23 show that he still believes God must judge the wicked; that is exactly why his own suffering is unbearable. On this view the debate collapses so that Job can turn from the friends to God (29–31). Against it: some passages still read awkwardly in Job's mouth.

The Plain keeps the Hebrew order and does not add "you say" or new speaker names. The notes at 24:18, 25:1, 26:5 and 27:13 give the proposed reassignments.

Eliphaz's list of crimes (22:6–9) and Job's later answer line up point by point:

  • Pledges taken from brothers for no reason (22:6); Job: his care for the poor man's covering (31:19–20).
  • The naked stripped (22:6); Job: he clothed the needy with his sheep's wool (31:19–20).
  • No water or bread for the weary and hungry (22:7); Job: he never ate his bread alone (31:17).
  • Widows sent away empty (22:9); Job: he made the widow's heart sing (29:13) and never dimmed her eyes (31:16).
  • The arms of the fatherless crushed (22:9); Job: he rescued the fatherless (29:12) and never raised his hand against them (31:21).

settings.by: Eliphaz the Temanite, who speaks first among the friends, perhaps as the eldest
settings.to: Job, sitting in his ruin, with Bildad and Zophar listening
settings.when: after Job has argued that the wicked live long and die at peace (21:7–34)
settings.why: To answer Job's claim that the wicked prosper by insisting that God is just, so Job's suffering must be deserved. Eliphaz names specific sins to make Job confess, then offers the way back: return to God and be restored. Knowing that the reader has seen the heavenly scene (1:6–12) turns his speech into a study of good doctrine wrongly applied.
settings.readers: For Israelites asking why the faithful suffer, perhaps in the aftermath of the exile, Eliphaz voices the answer they heard most often: suffering is punishment, so repent. The book lets that answer speak at full strength, and then shows it slandering an innocent man.
views: Many readers see the friends as voices of the standard wisdom of Proverbs and Deuteronomy, which the book tests and finds incomplete.
Others say the friends misuse sound teaching: Proverbs and Deuteronomy never say every sufferer is a sinner.

title: If Only I Could Find Him
sum: Job does not answer Eliphaz's charges. He speaks past him, about God. If only he could find God's seat, he would lay out his case, and God would listen; an upright man could reason with him and walk free (23:3–7). But Job searches forward and back, left and right, and finds no one (23:8–9).

Still, he trusts that God knows his road. Once God has tested him, he will come out like gold, for he has kept God's way and treasured his words (23:10–12). Then the confidence turns to terror: God is one, and does what he wants; that is why Job dreads him (23:13–17).
readings: Read as a lawsuit
Job's language is legal: a case, pleas, an upright man reasoning with a judge, an acquittal. Job believes justice exists, and that God, if met in court, would be just. His problem is access.
Read as the hidden God

Christian and Jewish readers have read this chapter as the classic text on God's hiddenness: the believer who seeks God everywhere and finds only silence, and who trusts anyway that God knows his way (23:10). Psalm 139 is its mirror image.

views.H: Job, a real man of Uz, speaks honestly out of real agony. Traditional readers take the speech as both true complaint and true faith.
views.C: Critics note that 23–24 is the last speech in the third round that is clearly Job's. They debate whether chapter 24 belongs with chapter 23, since 23 is personal and 24 is about the world.
views.W: The Babylonian sufferer in Ludlul bel nemeqi ("I Will Praise the Lord of Wisdom") says no one can know the will of the gods in heaven or understand their plans. Job shares the complaint but holds on to the hope of a hearing.
views.J: Jewish thought links the chapter to hester panim, the hiding of God's face (Deuteronomy 31:17–18), a theme that became central in reflection after the Holocaust.
views.X: 23:10 became one of the best-loved verses of Christian devotion, read as suffering that purifies (1 Peter 1:6–7). Gregory the Great read the search in 23:8–9 as the soul's search for a God who is everywhere and yet beyond reach. Calvin preached that Job was right to trust God's knowledge but wrong to demand that God appear in court.

settings.by: Job (24:18–24 is assigned to Zophar or Bildad by many scholars, or read as Job quoting the friends)
settings.to: Eliphaz and the friends, though much of it is spoken about God, as if to anyone who will listen
settings.when: after Eliphaz has accused him of crimes against the poor and urged him to return to God (22)
settings.why: Job refuses Eliphaz's offer, because returning would mean confessing sins he did not commit. He wants a trial, not forgiveness. In chapter 24 he widens his complaint from his own case to the whole world: the poor are robbed and God does nothing. The speech presses the question the book exists to ask.
settings.readers: Readers who had lost land, family and temple could hear their own cry in 24:1: why does God set no day of justice? The book lets Job say it without rebuke from the narrator.
views: Dhorme, Pope and others: 24:18–24 belongs to a friend's lost speech, displaced when the third round was damaged.
Gordis and others: Job quotes what the friends say; the RSV and ESV add "You say" at 24:18, which the Hebrew lacks.
Job curses the wicked, or grants that they do die in the end, but like everyone else (24:24).

title: Why Does God Keep No Court Days?
sum: Job's question widens: why does the Almighty set no times of judgment, so that the faithful can see justice done (24:1)? He describes what goes on in the meantime. Landgrabbers move boundary stones, steal flocks, and take the widow's ox and the orphan's donkey in pledge. The poor are pushed off the road, forage in the desert like wild donkeys, harvest other men's fields naked and hungry, and tread the winepresses thirsty. In the city the dying cry out, and God takes no notice (24:2–12).

Then come the rebels against the light: the murderer, the adulterer and the burglar, who work in the dark (24:13–17). The last section (24:18–24) suddenly describes the wicked carried off on the water and taken by Sheol, the view of Job's friends. Job ends by daring anyone to prove him a liar (24:25).
readings: Read as social protest

Chapter 24 is one of the Bible's most detailed pictures of rural poverty and its causes: debt, seized land, unpaid labor. It stands beside Amos and Micah, but with a difference: the prophets blame the rich and promise God's judgment; Job blames God for not judging.
Read as a disordered text

The ending (24:18–24) contradicts the rest of the chapter, and the Hebrew is very hard. Many scholars think it belongs to a friend's speech. Others hear Job quoting the friends, or conceding that the wicked do die, but no sooner than anyone else (24:24). See the deep dive on the chapter 22 page.

views.H: The details (boundary stones, pledges, terrace presses, mud-brick walls) fit village life in the ancient Levant, and traditional readers take them as what Job saw.
views.C: Most critics treat 24:18–24 (sometimes 24:18–25) as displaced, often assigned to Zophar's missing speech. Some also move 24:9 after 24:3. The verses 24:13–17 are sometimes seen as an independent poem.
views.W: In the Babylonian Theodicy the sufferer complains that the rich oppress the weak and the gods do nothing; the friend answers that the wicked will soon be cut down. Chapter 24 contains both voices, which supports either the quotation view or the reconstruction view.
views.J: Medieval Jewish commentators differ on 24:18–24: some read it as Job describing the eventual fate of the wicked while denying that it comes promptly, others as Job's curse on them.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 24:12, "the wounded gasp out cries for help," the cry of the oppressed that God hears in Exodus 3:7 and in Revelation 6:10, "how long?" Gregory read the night-workers of 24:13–17 as sinners who hate the light of truth (John 3:20).

echoes: 21:7–34; 22:6–9; Exodus 22:21–27; Deuteronomy 19:14; Deuteronomy 24:6–22; Deuteronomy 27:17; Amos 2:6–8; Habakkuk 1:2–4; John 3:19–20; Revelation 6:10

title: Bildad's Last Word
sum: Bildad speaks only five verses. God rules with dread and makes peace in the heights; his troops cannot be counted, and his light rises on everyone (25:2–3). How then can a human be in the right with God? If even the moon and stars are not pure in his eyes, how much less a human, a maggot, a mortal, a worm (25:4–6)!

It is the last speech any friend makes. Zophar, who should come next, never speaks. Whether Bildad's speech was cut short in the copying, or the author shows the friends running out of words, readers have debated for centuries (see the chapter 22 page).
readings: Read as the end of argument
Bildad no longer answers Job; he repeats what Eliphaz said in 4:17 and 15:14. The friends have nothing new. Their last word is that humans are worms, which may be true but does not touch Job's case.
Read as a fragment
Many scholars take 26:5–14, a hymn on God's power over the underworld, the sky and the sea, as the rest of Bildad's speech, which would make it as long as the others.

views.H: Bildad the Shuhite is from Shuah, perhaps linked to a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Traditional readers take his short speech as the friend falling silent.
views.C: The brevity is the strongest evidence that the third round is damaged. Most critical reconstructions add 26:5–14 to Bildad.
views.W: A Sumerian lament known as "A Man and His God" (early second millennium BC) says that no sinless child has ever been born to its mother, the same conviction as 25:4. In that text the sufferer confesses and is restored; Job refuses to confess what he did not do.
views.J: The line "in his heights he makes peace" (25:2) closes the Kaddish and the Amidah, in the form of a prayer: may he who makes peace in his heights make peace for us. Rashi reads it of God keeping peace between the angels of fire and of water.
views.X: Christian theologians have cited 25:4–6 for the universal sinfulness of humanity (Romans 3:23). Calvin preached that Bildad's doctrine was true but wrongly used. The verse is part of the debate between Christian traditions over how deep human corruption goes (see below).

traditions.q: How deep does human sinfulness go? ("How can anyone born of a woman be clean?" 25:4)
views: Human nature is wholly corrupted by the Fall, so that no one can do any good that pleases God without regenerating grace; texts like Job 25:4 and Job 15:14 are cited for this (Westminster Confession 6.2–4).
Original sin is a true sin that condemns, and it leaves human beings unable by nature to fear or trust God; only the gospel makes anyone clean before God (Augsburg Confession 2).
Original sin is a deprivation of original holiness, not a total corruption: human nature is wounded and inclined to sin, but not totally corrupted (Catechism 405).
Humans inherit mortality and a tendency to sin from Adam, but not Adam's guilt; the image of God is obscured, not destroyed (as Kallistos Ware summarizes).
All are born corrupt, but God's prevenient grace, given to everyone, restores enough freedom to respond to him (John Wesley, The Doctrine of Original Sin).

settings.to: Job, with the other friends listening
settings.when: after Job's complaint that God sets no days of judgment (23–24)
settings.why: To silence Job's demand for a trial by reminding him that no human can be clean before God. If even the moon and stars are impure to him, a maggot like Job has no standing to complain. The speech gives up on proving Job's particular guilt and falls back on universal guilt.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, Bildad's words were familiar piety, close to psalms of confession. The book shows that a true statement about human sinfulness can still be the wrong answer to a particular sufferer.
views: The speech originally continued, probably in 26:5–14, and was damaged.
The author shows the friends exhausted; Job interrupts Bildad (26:2).

title: The Edges of His Ways
sum: Job mocks Bildad: what a help you have been to the powerless, what wisdom you have shown the fool! Whose breath was speaking through you (26:2–4)? Then comes a hymn to God's power. The shades of the dead writhe beneath the waters; Sheol and Abaddon lie naked before him. He spreads the north over the void and hangs the earth on nothing, binds the waters in clouds, veils his throne, and draws the horizon where light meets darkness (26:5–10).

The pillars of heaven tremble at his rebuke. By his power he quelled the sea and struck down Rahab; his hand ran through the fleeing snake (26:11–13). Yet these are only the edges of his ways, a faint whisper of him. Who could take in his thunder in its full might (26:14)?
readings: Read as Job outdoing Bildad
Job, not Bildad, sings the hymn: you talk of God's greatness? I know it better than you. The final line shows Job's point: God's power is beyond understanding, which makes his silence all the harder.
Read as Bildad's lost speech
The hymn, especially 26:5–14, fits Bildad's theme (25:2–3) and would complete his short speech. On this view Job's answer is only 26:1–4 and resumes in chapter 27.

views.H: Traditional readers take the hymn as Job's own praise, showing that his complaint never denied God's majesty.
views.C: Many critics give 26:5–14 to Bildad. The cosmology (the waters under the earth, the pillars of heaven, the horizon as a circle) is the common picture of the ancient Near East.
views.W: The defeat of Sea and the serpent (26:12–13) uses the language of the Ugaritic Baal cycle, where Baal defeats Yam and the seven-headed serpent Lotan, described with the same words as Isaiah 27:1. Babylon's Enuma Elish tells of Marduk splitting the sea monster Tiamat. Job's hymn borrows the images for the one God.
views.J: The rabbis read 26:7, "hangs the earth on nothing," with wonder; the Talmud (Chullin 89a) says the world stands on the merit of those who keep their mouths shut in a quarrel, reading belimah, "nothing," as "restraint."
views.X: Church fathers such as Basil, in his homilies on the six days of creation, cited 26:7. Gregory the Great read 26:14 as the limit of all human knowledge of God, who is known in his works only as a whisper. Modern Christian readers sometimes read 26:7 as foreknowledge of an earth in space; most commentators take it as poetry.

settings.by: Job (26:5–14 is assigned to Bildad by many scholars)
settings.why: To mock Bildad's empty comfort, and then to show that Job knows God's power as well as any friend. If 26:5–14 is Job's, he shows that his complaint is not ignorance of God's greatness; that greatness is the problem. If it is Bildad's, the friend ends with a hymn that unwittingly prepares for God's own speech from the storm.
settings.readers: Israelite readers knew this language from their own psalms of creation and of God's victory over the sea (Psalm 74; Psalm 89; Psalm 104). They would hear Job using their own worship to press his case.
views: The Hebrew gives the whole chapter to Job; many readers keep it so.
Dhorme, Pope, Clines and others join it to 25:1–6.

title: I Will Not Let Go of My Integrity
sum: Job takes an oath by the life of the very God who, he says, has stripped him of his right: as long as he has breath, he will not speak a lie. He will never grant that his friends are right, and he will not set aside his integrity until he dies; his conscience finds no fault with any day of his life (27:2–6). Let his accuser be treated like the wicked, for what hope does the godless man have when God cuts him off (27:7–10)?

Then Job offers to teach the friends about God's hand, and describes the share the wicked receive from God: children lost to the sword and plague, silver heaped up for the righteous to share, a house as fragile as a moth's, and an east wind that whirls him away while people clap and hiss (27:11–23). The words are almost those of Zophar (20:29), and readers have long asked why Job says them.
readings: Read as Job's oath

27:2–6 is Job's first formal oath of innocence, and it sets up chapter 31. To admit guilt he does not feel would be a lie, and so a betrayal of the very integrity God praised (2:3). Honesty before God is, for Job, a form of faith.
Read as the friends' doctrine in Job's mouth

27:13–23 sounds like the friends. It may be Zophar's lost third speech, Job quoting the friends in order to turn their doctrine on them, or Job confessing that he too believes God will judge the wicked in the end. See the deep dive on the chapter 22 page.

views.H: Traditional readers take the whole chapter as Job's, and read 27:13–23 as his true belief that the wicked will be judged, though not as quickly as the friends claim.
views.C: The new heading (27:1), with no friend speaking in between, is taken by many critics as a sign that Zophar's third speech has been lost or absorbed. Most reconstructions give him 27:13–23, sometimes with 27:7–10.
views.W: Oaths of innocence before a god are known from Mesopotamian and Egyptian legal practice. The wicked man's fate in 27:13–23 is a stock theme of ancient wisdom, as in the Babylonian Theodicy's promise that the oppressor will soon be cut down.
views.J: The Mishnah records a debate about Job's motive. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai taught that Job served God out of fear; Rabbi Joshua ben Hyrcanus answered that he served out of love, citing Job's oath in this chapter: until he dies he will not set his integrity aside (27:5; Mishnah Sotah 5:5).
views.X: Christian readers have admired 27:5–6 as a model of a clear conscience (Acts 24:16; 1 John 3:21). Calvin warned that a clear conscience before humans is not the same as purity before God's hidden righteousness. Aquinas read the chapter as Job defending not his sinlessness but his freedom from the great sins the friends charged.

settings.what: Job's oath and his poem on the wicked man's share
settings.by: Job (27:13–23, and sometimes 27:7–12, is assigned to Zophar by many scholars)
settings.to: the three friends (the "you" of 27:5, 11–12 is plural)
settings.when: after Bildad's short speech and Job's reply (25–26), when Zophar's turn would come
settings.why: To put his innocence under oath, the strongest statement a person could make in an ancient court, so that the friends must either accept it or call down God's judgment. If 27:13–23 is Job's, he reminds the friends that the wicked do face God's judgment, and that false accusers (27:7) should fear it.
settings.readers: Israelite readers knew oaths "by the life of the LORD" from their courts and stories (Ruth 3:13; 1 Samuel 14:39). Here a man swears by God against God's apparent verdict, which set the book's first readers a question they could not ignore: can a faithful person protest to God and stay faithful?
views: Gordis and others: 27:13–23 is the friends' doctrine on Job's lips.
Dhorme, Pope, Clines and others: the verses are Zophar's.
Andersen, Hartley: Job believes the wicked will be judged; that is why his case baffles him.

title: Where Can Wisdom Be Found?
sum: A quiet poem interrupts the storm of argument. Humans are brilliant: they dig mines for silver and gold, smelt iron and copper, carry lamps to the ends of the darkness, hang on ropes in shafts far from any village, cut channels through rock and dam underground springs. No bird of prey or lion has ever seen the paths they open (28:1–11).

But wisdom: where can it be found? It is not in the land of the living, not in the Deep or the Sea, and no gold, gems, coral or pearls can buy it. Even Abaddon and Death have only heard a rumor of it (28:12–22). God alone knows the way to it, for he saw it and set it in place when he gave the wind its weight and the rain its law. And he said to humankind: the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and to keep away from evil is understanding (28:23–28).
readings: Read as an interlude

The poem pauses the drama between the failed debate (3–27) and Job's closing speeches (29–31). It tells the reader what none of the speakers has grasped: true wisdom belongs to God, and humans receive only reverence and goodness. It points ahead to God's speech from the storm (38–41).
Read as Job's speech

In the Hebrew order Job is still speaking (27:1). On this reading Job, having rejected the friends' wisdom, now says that no human has the answer, himself included, and returns to the simple piety of 1:1. Chapters 29–31 then show him holding that piety and still demanding an answer.
Read as a wisdom hymn

The poem stands beside Proverbs 8, Sirach 24, Baruch 3:9–4:4 and the Wisdom of Solomon 7–9, the great poems about Wisdom in Jewish tradition. Unlike them, Job 28 does not make wisdom a woman who comes to dwell with Israel. It stays hidden with God.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as Job's own words, a sign that his faith in God's wisdom survives his complaint. The mining details reflect real practices of the ancient Near East.
views.C: Most critics doubt that Job speaks the poem, since its calm tone and its answer seem to settle the debate before God speaks. They see it as the author's interlude (Westermann, Habel, Newsom), a later addition, or a misplaced part of Elihu's speeches (Clines moves it after chapter 37). Some also think 28:28 was added to align the poem with Proverbs. The Old Greek lacked about a third of the poem, probably cut by the translator (see the note at 28:21).
views.W: Mesopotamian wisdom also says the gods' wisdom is hidden: the Babylonian Theodicy says the mind of the god is as remote as the middle of the heavens. Ancient mining is attested at Timna and Faynan in the Arabah, and Egyptian expeditions mined turquoise and copper in Sinai.
views.J: Jewish tradition identified the wisdom of Job 28 with the Torah, as Baruch 3:9–4:1 already does. The verse "the fear of the Lord is wisdom" became a motto of Jewish ethical teaching.
views.X: Christian readers connected the hidden wisdom of Job 28 with Christ, whom Paul calls God's power and God's wisdom (1 Corinthians 1:24), the one in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden (Colossians 2:3). Gregory the Great and Aquinas read 28:28 as the summary of the moral life.

deep.b:
The Hebrew gives no new speaker: Job "took up his poem again" at 27:1, and the next heading is the same at 29:1. So in the text as it stands, chapter 28 is Job's. Four views:

The narrator's interlude. Many scholars (Westermann, Habel, Newsom, and others) hear the voice of the author pausing the drama. The poem is calm where Job is anguished; it speaks of "humans" in general, not of Job; and it gives the answer that only God will give in 38–41. Like a chorus in a Greek play, it tells the reader what the characters do not yet know.

Job's own speech. Others (Andersen, Janzen, and many traditional readers) keep it as Job's. Having heard every argument, Job confesses that wisdom is beyond everyone, and returns to the reverence and goodness he lived by (1:1). His closing defense (29–31) then shows that a man can fear God and still ask God for an answer.

A misplaced or added poem. Some think it is a separate wisdom poem placed here by an editor. Clines moves it to the end of Elihu's speeches, where its theme fits Elihu's claim to teach wisdom (32–37).

A deliberate bridge. Newsom and others note that, whoever speaks it, the poem marks the end of the dialogue's search for wisdom and turns the book toward the voice from the storm.

The Plain keeps the poem where it stands, without a new speaker, and closes Job's speech at 28:28.

deep.h: The poem and later wisdom writings
deep.b:
Job 28 became a model for later Jewish poems about wisdom:

  • Proverbs 8:22–31 pictures Wisdom as a figure present with God at creation, delighting in humankind. Job 28 has God see and set wisdom at creation, but it never becomes a person.
  • Baruch 3:9–4:4 (deuterocanonical: Scripture for Catholic and Orthodox Christians, the Apocrypha for Protestants) asks who has gone up to heaven to find wisdom, who has crossed the sea for her, and answers that God alone knows her and gave her to Israel as the book of God's commandments.
  • Sirach 24 (also deuterocanonical) has Wisdom seek a home among all nations, then settle in Jerusalem as the Torah of Moses.
  • The Wisdom of Solomon 7–9 (deuterocanonical) calls wisdom a vapor rising from God's power and asks God to send her to the king.

All of these bring wisdom down to Israel. Job 28 leaves it hidden with God and gives humans only its practical form: fear the Lord and keep away from evil.

echoes: 1:1; 1:8; 11:7–9; 12:13; 38:1–39:30; Proverbs 1:7; Proverbs 3:13–20; Proverbs 8:22–31; Ecclesiastes 7:23–24; Baruch 3:9–4:4; Sirach 1:1–10; Sirach 24:1–23; Wisdom of Solomon 7:25–8:1; 1 Corinthians 1:24; Colossians 2:3

settings.by: Job in the Hebrew order; many scholars hear the narrator or author
settings.to: the friends and the reader; if it is an interlude, the reader alone
settings.when: between Job's oath (27) and his closing defense (29–31), after the friends have fallen silent
settings.why: To show that the debate could not succeed: neither Job nor his friends can find wisdom by searching, as miners find silver. God alone knows it. What humans can do is fear the Lord and keep away from evil, which is exactly how the prologue describes Job (1:1). The poem prepares for God's answer from the storm (38–41).
settings.readers: For Jewish readers, perhaps after the exile (the book's date is debated), who were building a life around the Torah as Israel's wisdom (as Baruch and Sirach would say), the poem offers a humble foundation: God's wisdom is beyond us, but reverence and goodness are within reach.

title: When God Watched Over Me
sum: Job begins his closing defense by remembering the old days: God's lamp over his head, God's friendship over his tent, his boys around him, his feet wading in curds (29:2–6). When he went up to the town gate, the young kept out of his way, the aged stood, and leaders and nobles fell silent (29:7–10).

They honored him because he rescued the poor and the fatherless, gave the widow's heart a song, was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, a father to the needy, and broke the jaws of the wrongdoer (29:11–17). He expected to die old in his nest, a well-watered tree (29:18–20). People waited for his words like farmers for spring rain, and he lived like a king among his troops, one who comforted the grieving (29:21–25).
readings: Read as testimony

Chapter 29 is Job's character evidence before the court. It answers Eliphaz's charges (22:6–9) and shows a man whose honor came from justice. Job is not boasting of wealth but of what he did with power.
Read as the portrait of a righteous ruler

Job's description matches the ideal king of the ancient Near East and of Israel's psalms (Psalm 72): protector of widows and orphans, judge at the gate, a giver of life like rain. A gentile elder lives the royal ideal in his town.

views.H: The chapter gives a vivid picture of a leading man's place in an ancient town: the gate, the square, the elders and nobles. Traditional readers take it as Job's true memory.
views.C: Critics see chapters 29–31 as a single composition, Job's final speech, perhaps once directly followed by God's answer (38:1), with Elihu (32–37) inserted later.
views.W: In the Ugaritic tale of Aqhat, the righteous Danel sits at the gate and judges the case of the widow and the orphan. Hammurabi's law code says he made his laws so the strong would not oppress the weak and the widow and orphan would get justice. Job's self-portrait belongs to this tradition.
views.J: The rabbis held Job up beside Abraham as a model of kindness. Avot de-Rabbi Natan (chapter 7) says Job's house had doors on all four sides so that the poor would not have to walk around to find the entrance. The Testament of Job, a Jewish retelling (in no Bible today), expands his charity at length.
views.X: Christian readers have compared 29:12–17 with Jesus' mission to bring good news to the poor and sight to the blind (Luke 4:18; Matthew 11:5), and with the works of mercy in Matthew 25:35–36.

settings.what: Job's closing defense: past honor, present shame, oath of innocence
settings.to: anyone who will hear (31:35): the silent friends, the court of public opinion, and above all God, whom he addresses directly in 30:20–23
settings.when: after the friends have fallen silent and the poem on wisdom (28)
settings.why: To lay his whole case before the court one last time: the honor he earned by justice (29), the disgrace he suffers now (30), and a sworn denial of every hidden sin (31). The speech is built to force a response: Job signs it and demands that God answer (31:35). Its form is close to the lament psalms, which move from memory to complaint to a claim of innocence.
settings.readers: For the book's first readers, Job's closing speech gave voice to the faithful who had kept God's ways and lost everything. It showed them that a full, honest account of one's life could be laid before God without pretending to guilt.

title: And Now They Mock Me
sum: "And now": the men who mock Job are young outcasts whose fathers he thought too low to rank with his sheepdogs. They once lived in the gullies of the wadis, gnawing roots and salty orache, driven out of every village (30:1–8). Now they make songs about him, spit at him, and pour in on him like soldiers through a breach, because God has slackened Job's cord (30:9–15).

Job turns to his body and to God. Pain gnaws his bones at night, his clothes no longer fit, God has thrown him in the mud. He cries out and God only looks at him; God has become cruel and bears him a grudge; he tosses Job in the storm and will send him back to death (30:16–23). Job wept for others in their hard days, but when he hoped for light, darkness came. He goes about in black, a brother to jackals, his skin black and coming off, his harp turned to mourning (30:24–31).
readings: Read as a lament

Chapter 30 has the shape of a lament psalm: the mockery of enemies (Psalm 22:6–8; Psalm 69:11–12), the body in pain (Psalm 38:3–8), the God who does not answer (Psalm 22:2). Unlike most laments, it ends with no turn to praise.
Read as social reversal

The man who sat at the gate now hears songs from the lowest people in the land. Job's contempt for these outcasts (30:1–8) is uncomfortable, and some readers find in it a hint of the pride that God's speech will humble. Others say it measures how far he has fallen.

views.H: Traditional readers take the chapter as Job's true experience of disgrace and of the disease that afflicted him (2:7–8).
views.C: Some critics think 30:2–8 is a separate poem about desert outcasts inserted here, since it matches 24:5–8. The Hebrew of 30:3–4, 11–14, 18 and 24 is among the hardest in the book.
views.W: The Babylonian sufferer of Ludlul bel nemeqi complains that his city frowns on him, his friends have turned against him, and the lowliest mock him, much as Job does. In Ludlul the god Marduk finally restores him.
views.J: The Testament of Job tells how Job's former neighbors and servants despised him. Rashi explains 30:2: Job had no use for the strength of these men even in his good days, because they were wicked and trouble came through them; he takes the rare word kelach as "old age," as in 5:26.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 30:9–10 (mocking songs, spitting in the face) the suffering of Christ (Mark 14:65; Mark 15:29–32; Isaiah 50:6), and Gregory the Great read Job throughout as a figure of Christ the sufferer.

settings.what: Job's lament over his present shame
settings.to: the hearers of his closing defense; in 30:20–23 he speaks directly to God
settings.when: the second part of the closing speech (29–31), after he has described his former honor
settings.why: To set his present disgrace beside his former honor, so that the injustice is plain. The direct address to God (30:20–23) is the speech's sharpest point: God is the one who has turned cruel. The lament prepares for the oath (31): if Job has done none of the things that could deserve this, God must answer.
settings.readers: Israel's psalms of lament gave the book's first readers a language for this kind of grief. Job uses it without the hopeful ending many psalms have, which let readers know that such grief could be brought to God unfinished.

title: Job's Oath of Innocence
sum: Job ends his defense with an oath. In the form of "if I did this, may that happen to me," he denies one sin after another: a lustful look, lies and dishonest dealing, adultery, brushing aside the complaints of his slaves, neglecting the poor, the widow and the fatherless, raising his hand in court against the orphan, trusting in gold, secretly worshiping the sun and moon, gloating over an enemy, turning away a stranger, hiding his sin as Adam did (31:1–34).

Then he signs it: "Here is my mark: now let the Almighty answer me!" Let his accuser write out the charge; Job would wear it like a crown and walk up to God like a prince (31:35–37). One more oath, about his land and its workers (31:38–40), and "Here Job's words come to an end." The next voice that answers Job, after Elihu, will be God's from the storm (38:1).
readings: Read as a legal challenge

In ancient law an accused person could clear himself by an oath, calling down a curse if he lied. If no curse fell, he was innocent, and his accuser had to answer. Job uses the oath to force God into court: either strike me or answer me (31:35).
Read as an ethic

Chapter 31 is the Bible's fullest description of a righteous private life. Many of its sins are inward or hidden, known only to God. It is often called the summit of Old Testament ethics, close to the Sermon on the Mount.
Read as pride

Some readers, ancient and modern, hear in the oath a man too sure of himself, who must be humbled by God's questions (38:2). Others answer that God himself called Job wholehearted (1:8) and later says Job spoke rightly (42:7).

views.H: Traditional readers take the oath as Job's true record, confirmed by God's own words about him (1:8; 2:3; 42:7–8).
views.C: Critics note that the oath matches both Israel's laws and older ancient Near Eastern forms. Many move 31:38–40 to an earlier place in the chapter. The date of the chapter, like the book, is usually set between the 600s and 300s BC.
views.W: Chapter 125 of the Egyptian Book of the Dead has the dead person deny 42 sins before Osiris and his judges, and the Babylonian Shurpu tablets list sins from which a sufferer asks release. Job's oath shares the form but is spoken to one God, in life, as a challenge.
views.J: The rabbis compared Job's hospitality (31:32) with Abraham's and, in one story, had God tell Job that he had not reached half of Abraham's measure, since Abraham went out to look for guests while Job waited for them to come (Avot de-Rabbi Natan, chapter 7). Ralbag and Maimonides read Job as a man of great moral virtue who lacked full knowledge of God's ways.
views.X: Christian readers have long set Job 31:1 beside Matthew 5:28, and 31:29–30 beside Matthew 5:43–44. Gregory the Great praised Job's virtues as real holiness. Calvin, in his Sermons on Job, said that Job was right against his friends but wrong to think he could stand before God's higher, hidden righteousness. The chapter sits at the center of a disagreement among Christians about righteousness and works (see below).

deep.h: Job's oath and the laws of Moses
deep.b:
Job is a man of Uz, not an Israelite, and the book never names Moses or Sinai. Yet nearly every oath in chapter 31 matches a law of the Torah, and many go beyond it to the heart. The site's Plain of those laws, beside Job's oaths:

  • The look of desire (31:1). "You must not crave your neighbor's wife" (Exodus 20:17). Job's covenant reaches the eye itself.
  • Lies and deceit; honest scales (31:5–6). "Do not steal. Do not deceive. Do not deal falsely, any of you, with his fellow citizen" (Leviticus 19:11). "Have scales that are right, weights that are right" (Leviticus 19:36).
  • Adultery (31:9–12). "You must not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14); a man who commits adultery with his neighbor's wife "must be put to death" (Leviticus 20:10).
  • Justice for slaves (31:13–15). "If someone hits his slave, man or woman, in the eye and ruins it, he must let the slave go free in exchange for the eye" (Exodus 21:26). The Sabbath rest is for "your slave, man or woman" too (Exodus 20:10).
  • The poor, the widow and the fatherless (31:16–20). "Never treat a widow or a fatherless child harshly" (Exodus 22:22). "Leave them for the poor and for the foreigner" (Leviticus 19:10). "Do not bend the justice due a foreigner or a fatherless child, and do not take a widow's garment as a pledge" (Deuteronomy 24:17). The poor man's coat comes back at sundown "so that he can sleep in his coat and bless you" (Deuteronomy 24:13), and Job says the poor man's body blessed him (31:20).
  • Power in court (31:21–22). "Do not push aside the right of the needy among you when his case is heard" (Exodus 23:6). "Do no wrong in judgment. Do not lift up the face of the poor man, and do not honor the face of the great man" (Leviticus 19:15).
  • Gold and the sun and moon (31:24–28). "You must not have any other gods in my presence" (Exodus 20:3). "Do not be pulled away to bow down to them and serve them" (Deuteronomy 4:19).
  • Joy at an enemy's ruin (31:29–30). "If you meet your enemy's ox or his donkey straying, you must bring it back to him" (Exodus 23:4). "Do not hate your brother in your heart" and "Do not take vengeance, and do not keep a grudge" (Leviticus 19:17–18).
  • The foreigner (31:32). "Do not mistreat a foreigner living among you" (Exodus 22:21). "You are to love him as yourself, because you were foreigners in the land of Egypt" (Leviticus 19:34).
  • The land and its workers (31:38–40). "The wages of a hired worker must not stay with you overnight until morning" (Leviticus 19:13). "Pay him his wages each day, before the sun goes down" (Deuteronomy 24:15).

Three things stand out. First, Job's list is heavy on inward and hidden sins: desire, trust in wealth, secret worship, private gloating. Several of these no court could ever try; only God sees them (31:4, 14, 23). Second, Job grounds his treatment of slaves not in a law but in creation: one Maker formed them both (31:15). Third, Job's oath is not a list of rules kept but of a life lived. That is why commentators call chapter 31 the high point of Old Testament ethics, the passage that comes closest to the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:27–28, 43–44).

Scholars disagree on what the parallels mean. Some think the poet, an Israelite, consciously built Job's oath from the Torah, so that Israelite readers would recognize a gentile who kept its spirit. Others think both the Torah and Job draw on a shared ethic of the ancient Near East, seen also in Egypt's Book of the Dead and Babylon's Shurpu lists (see the note at 31:5).

Each section follows a pattern: "If I have done X" (the condition), and then "may Y happen to me" (the self-curse). Not every "if" gets its curse; in Hebrew, an oath can leave the curse unspoken ("may God do so to me"), as in 1 Samuel 3:17 and Ruth 1:17. The spoken curses match the crimes: if his eyes led his heart, may another eat his crops (31:7–8); if he lusted after another man's wife, may his own be taken (31:9–10); if his arm was raised against the fatherless, may it be torn off (31:21–22); if he took the land unjustly, may it grow thorns (31:38–40). Michael Dick has argued that the chapter follows the form of a legal oath meant to force the plaintiff to bring formal charges or drop the case.

traditions.q: Does Job's oath (31) show a righteousness that God accepts because of works?
views: Job's righteousness is real. Good works done by a person living in God's grace are truly good and, by God's promise, truly merit reward (Council of Trent, Session 6, chapter 16 and canon 32; Catechism 2006–2011). Gregory the Great's Moralia treats Job's virtues as genuine holiness.

The Church honors "the holy and righteous Job" (commemorated on May 6) as a saint. Righteousness is a real sharing in God's holiness through cooperation with grace (synergy), not a legal standing; Job's life shows that holiness, though no one is sinless before God.

Job's integrity is a civil righteousness, true before other people, and it rightly clears him of the friends' charges. Before God no one is justified by works but only by faith in God's promise (Augsburg Confession 4; Apology 4). Job is right before humans, and in need of grace before God.

Calvin's Sermons on Job distinguish a righteousness of the law, which Job kept, from God's higher, hidden righteousness, by which even angels would fall short. Job was right in his cause against the friends, but no one can claim standing before God by works (Westminster Confession 16.5).

John Wesley taught that believers can, by grace, be made perfect in love, free from willful sin; Job's oath shows what that blamelessness of intention looks like, without claiming freedom from all faults (Wesley, Christian Perfection).

settings.to: God above all, whom he summons to answer (31:35); also the friends and the elders of the town, before whom such oaths were sworn
settings.when: the end of Job's closing defense (29–31), the last words of Job before God speaks
settings.why: To clear himself under oath of every sin that could explain his suffering, including hidden ones no human court could try, and so to force God to answer: either the curses fall, or God must give his charge or acquit him. The oath shows a gentile living by the spirit of laws Israel knew from Sinai.
settings.readers: For Israelite readers who knew Exodus, Leviticus and Deuteronomy, Job's oath was a mirror: here was the life the Torah asked for, lived by a man of Uz. It also gave the faithful sufferer permission to say "I have not done this" without being called proud.
views: Dick and others: the oath is a formal device to force God into court.
A confession of a whole life
Others read it as moral testimony more than legal strategy.
